summary.text: Split the admissible sequences by whether the first two entries form a non-ascent or an ascent: deleting the first entry in the former case has two inverses (prepend the remaining maximum or its successor), while in the latter the first two entries must be consecutive and deleting both again has two inverses. Thus the counts satisfy \(b_L=2b_{L-1}+2b_{L-2}\); the direct initial counts \(b_1=1\) and \(b_2=3\) identify them with the desired recurrence sequence.

full_proof.text:
Let a sequence of length \(L\) mean an ordered tuple
\[
 x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_L)
\]
of positive integers. Call such a sequence valid if it has the following two properties.

1. If \(M=\max_i x_i\), then every integer in the initial interval \(\{1,2,\ldots,M\}\) occurs among the entries of \(x\).
2. Whenever \(j\ge i+2\), one has \(x_i\ge x_j\). Thus entries in non-adjacent positions, read from left to right, are weakly decreasing.

Let \(C_L\) denote the number of valid sequences of length \(L\). We will prove
\[
 C_1=1,\qquad C_2=3,
\]
and, for every \(L\ge3\),
\[
 C_L=2C_{L-1}+2C_{L-2}. \tag{1}
\]
Since A028859 is defined by
\[
 a(0)=1,\qquad a(1)=3,\qquad
 a(n+2)=2a(n+1)+2a(n), \tag{2}
\]
these identities imply \(C_{n+1}=a(n)\) for every \(n\ge0\), which is precisely the claimed interpretation.

We first note that all the sets being counted are finite. If a valid sequence has length \(L\) and maximum \(M\), then the \(M\) distinct values \(1,2,\ldots,M\) all occur in its \(L\) positions. Hence \(M\le L\). In particular, every entry lies in \(\{1,\ldots,L\}\), so there are only finitely many valid sequences of a fixed length.

We now establish the structural decomposition that gives (1). Fix a valid sequence
\[
 x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_L)
\]
of length \(L\ge3\). There are two main cases, according as the first step is a non-ascent or an ascent.

### Case I: \(x_2\le x_1\)

For every \(j\ge3\), positions \(1\) and \(j\) are non-adjacent, so the defining monotonicity condition gives \(x_j\le x_1\). Together with \(x_2\le x_1\), this shows that \(x_1\) is a maximum of the entire sequence.

Let
\[
 \tau=(x_2,x_3,\ldots,x_L)
\]
be the tail, and put
\[
 S=\max \tau.
\]
We claim first that \(\tau\) is valid. Its entries are positive, and its non-adjacent monotonicity condition is inherited directly from that of \(x\). It remains to check that it covers every integer from \(1\) through \(S\).

Take \(k\) with \(1\le k\le S\). Since \(S\le x_1=\max x\), validity of \(x\) ensures that \(k\) occurs somewhere in \(x\). If it occurs after the first position, then it occurs in \(\tau\), as required. The only possible difficulty is that an occurrence supplied by the covering property is at the first position, so that \(k=x_1\). But then
\[
 S\le x_1=k\le S,
\]
so \(k=S\). Because the nonempty finite tail \(\tau\) attains its maximum \(S\), the value \(k=S\) occurs in \(\tau\) after all. Thus \(\tau\) covers \(\{1,\ldots,S\}\), and is valid.

We next determine the possible value of the deleted first entry. Since \(x_1\) is at least every tail entry, \(S\le x_1\). On the other hand,
\[
 x_1\le S+1. \tag{3}
\]
Indeed, if \(x_1=1\), (3) is immediate. If \(x_1>1\), then the covering property for \(x\) says that \(x_1-1\) occurs. It cannot occur only as the first entry, whose value is \(x_1\), so it occurs in the tail. Consequently \(x_1-1\le S\), which is equivalent to (3). Therefore
\[
 x_1=S \quad\hbox{or}\quad x_1=S+1. \tag{4}
\]

Conversely, start with any valid sequence \(\tau\) of length \(L-1\), let \(S=\max\tau\), choose \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and prepend
\[
 v=S+b.
\]
The resulting sequence
\[
 (v,\tau)

a
\]
(where the isolated “a” is to be ignored; the tuple is simply \((v,\tau)\)) is valid. More explicitly, all entries are positive because \(S\ge1\). Its maximum is \(v\). If \(b=0\), the tail already covers every value through \(v=S\). If \(b=1\), the tail covers every value through \(S=v-1\), while the new first entry supplies \(v\). Thus the initial-interval condition holds in both cases. For the non-adjacent monotonicity condition, comparisons wholly inside the tail follow from validity of \(\tau\), while any required comparison involving the new first entry has a later tail value on the right, and every such value is at most \(S\le v\). Finally, the new second entry is at most \(S\le v\), so the resulting sequence lies in the present non-ascent case.

Deletion of the first entry and this prepending operation are inverse to one another once \(b\) is fixed. Indeed, (4) determines \(b=x_1-S\) uniquely, and the deleted tail together with \(b\) reconstructs \(x_1=S+b\). Hence the valid sequences in Case I form two disjoint classes, each in bijection with the valid sequences of length \(L-1\). Case I therefore contributes
\[
 2C_{L-1}. \tag{5}
\]

### Case II: \(x_1<x_2\)

For every \(j\ge3\), positions \(1\) and \(j\) are non-adjacent, and hence
\[
 x_j\le x_1<x_2.
\]
Thus \(x_2\) is the maximum of the whole sequence.

In fact,
\[
 x_2=x_1+1. \tag{6}
\]
To see this, suppose instead that \(x_2\ge x_1+2\). Since \(x_2\) is the maximum and the sequence covers every value up to its maximum, the value \(x_1+1\) must occur. It is not at position \(1\), whose value is \(x_1\), and it is not at position \(2\), whose value is at least \(x_1+2\). It also cannot occur at any position \(j\ge3\), because all such entries are at most \(x_1\). This contradiction proves (6).

Delete the first two terms, writing
\[
 \upsilon=(x_3,x_4,\ldots,x_L),
 \qquad S=\max\upsilon.
\]
We claim that \(\upsilon\) is valid. Positivity and non-adjacent monotonicity are inherited from \(x\). Moreover, as observed above, every entry from position \(3\) onward is at most \(x_1\), so
\[
 S\le x_1. \tag{7}
\]
Now let \(1\le k\le S\). The original sequence contains \(k\). It cannot occur at the second position because
\[
 x_2=x_1+1>x_1\ge S\ge k.
\]
If it occurs at some position from \(3\) onward, it is already in \(\upsilon\). The remaining possibility is that it occurs at the first position, so \(k=x_1\). In that event (7) and \(k\le S\) force \(k=x_1=S\); since \(S\) is the maximum of the nonempty finite sequence \(\upsilon\), it occurs in \(\upsilon\). Thus every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,S\}\) occurs in \(\upsilon\), proving that \(\upsilon\) is valid.

We also have
\[
 x_1=S \quad\hbox{or}\quad x_1=S+1. \tag{8}
\]
The lower bound \(S\le x_1\) is (7). For the upper bound, if \(x_1=1\), then certainly \(x_1\le S+1\). If \(x_1>1\), the value \(x_1-1\) must occur because the original sequence covers its initial interval. It is neither \(x_1\) at the first position nor \(x_1+1\) at the second position, by (6), so it must occur in \(\upsilon\). Therefore \(x_1-1\le S\), or \(x_1\le S+1\). Together with (7), this proves (8).

Conversely, let \(\upsilon\) be any valid sequence of length \(L-2\), let \(S=\max\upsilon\), and choose \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Set
\[
 v=S+b
\]
and prepend the two entries \(v,v+1\), obtaining
\[
 (v,v+1,\upsilon). \tag{9}
\]
This is valid. All entries are positive. Its maximum is \(v+1\). If \(b=0\), then \(\upsilon\) covers \(1,\ldots,S=v\), and the newly inserted second entry supplies \(v+1\). If \(b=1\), then \(\upsilon\) covers \(1,\ldots,S\), while the two inserted entries supply \(S+1=v\) and \(S+2=v+1\). Hence (9) covers every value through its maximum in either case.

For the non-adjacent monotonicity condition, comparisons wholly within \(\upsilon\) are already valid. Every term of \(\upsilon\) is at most \(S\le v\), so every required comparison from the first inserted entry \(v\) to a term of \(\upsilon\) holds. Likewise every required comparison from the second inserted entry \(v+1\) to a non-adjacent later term holds. The first two inserted positions are adjacent, so no decreasing condition is imposed between them; indeed, they form the required ascent \(v<v+1\).

For a sequence in Case II, equations (6) and (8) show that its first two entries are uniquely reconstructed from its double tail and the unique bit \(b=x_1-S\): they are \(S+b,S+b+1\). Thus deleting the first two entries gives, for each fixed \(b\in\{0,1\}\), a bijection with valid sequences of length \(L-2\). The two values of \(b\) give disjoint classes. Case II therefore contributes
\[
 2C_{L-2}. \tag{10}
\]

The alternatives \(x_2\le x_1\) and \(x_1<x_2\) are exhaustive and disjoint. Within each alternative, the two values \(b=0,1\) are also disjoint because they give different equations for the deleted initial term. Combining (5) and (10) proves the recurrence
\[
 C_L=2C_{L-1}+2C_{L-2}
\]
for every \(L\ge3\).

It remains to establish the initial values. For length \(1\), a valid sequence must be \((1)\). Indeed, if its sole value were at least \(2\), the covering condition would require the distinct value \(1\) to occur as well, which is impossible. Thus
\[
 C_1=1.
\]
For length \(2\), the non-adjacent condition is vacuous, because the two positions are adjacent. The covering condition implies that the maximum is at most \(2\), and positivity leaves only values \(1\) and \(2\). Moreover, the value \(1\) must occur. The possibilities are exactly
\[
 (1,1),\qquad(1,2),\qquad(2,1),
\]
so
\[
 C_2=3.
\]

We can now identify the counts with A028859. We prove by induction on \(n\) that
\[
 C_{n+1}=a(n). \tag{11}
\]
For \(n=0\), this is \(C_1=1=a(0)\); for \(n=1\), it is \(C_2=3=a(1)\). If (11) holds at \(n=m\) and \(n=m+1\), then the recurrence for \(C_L\), applied with \(L=m+3\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 C_{m+3}
 &=2C_{m+2}+2C_{m+1}\\
 &=2a(m+1)+2a(m)\\
 &=a(m+2),
\end{aligned}
\]
where the last equality is the defining recurrence (2). This completes the induction.

For completeness, the same recurrence also explains the canonical description of A028859 as counting ternary strings with no consecutive zeros. Let \(T_n\) be the number of words of length \(n\) over \(\{0,1,2\}\) which avoid \(00\). Clearly \(T_0=1\) and \(T_1=3\). For \(n\ge2\), a valid word either ends in \(1\) or \(2\), giving \(2T_{n-1}\) possibilities after choosing an arbitrary valid prefix of length \(n-1\), or it ends in \(0\). In the latter case its penultimate symbol must be \(1\) or \(2\), and deleting those final two symbols leaves an arbitrary valid word of length \(n-2\), giving \(2T_{n-2}\) possibilities. Hence
\[
 T_n=2T_{n-1}+2T_{n-2},
\]
with the same initial values as \(a(n)\), so \(T_n=a(n)\).

Therefore, for every \(n\ge0\), the number \(a(n)\)—equivalently, the number of ternary strings of length \(n\) avoiding consecutive zeros—is exactly the number of length-\(n+1\) positive-integer sequences which cover an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing.
